Timeline::is_leap_year¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

Series Timeline::is_leap_year() const

What The Predicate Asks¶

is_leap_year() classifies the local civil year containing each instant. It returns true for every instant in a 366-day Gregorian year, not only for 29 February. This makes it useful before calendar arithmetic whose result may depend on February’s length, or when partitioning observations by calendar type.

The complete Gregorian rule is used: years divisible by four are leap years, except century years are common years unless divisible by 400. Consequently, 1900 and 2100 are common years while 2000 is a leap year.

Result Contract¶

The result is a newly allocated boolean Series with exactly the receiver’s rank and shape. A scalar Timeline produces a rank-zero Series; a matrix produces a matrix; an empty extent remains empty. NaT maps to false, so use isvalid() as a second mask when an absent instant must remain distinguishable from an instant in a common year.

The receiver is not modified. The timezone is read as calendar context: the same stored instant can belong to different local years after tz_convert(). The operation performs one pass over the values and loads timezone rules once for the call.

Example 1: Classify Years, Not Leap Days¶

const auto calendar = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2019-12-31T12:00:00Z", "2020-01-01T12:00:00Z",
    "2020-02-29T12:00:00Z", "2020-03-31T12:00:00Z",
    "2020-04-01T12:00:00Z", "2020-12-31T12:00:00Z",
    "2021-01-01T12:00:00Z", "2024-02-29T12:00:00Z", "",
});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, calendar.is_leap_year());

Series(shape=[9], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=9, contiguous=true)
data=[false, true, true, true, true, true, false, true, false]

Every 2020 instant is true. The final false represents NaT, not a known common year.

Example 2: Century Exceptions¶

const auto centuries = pluss::timeline::make({
    "1900-06-15T12:00:00Z",
    "2000-06-15T12:00:00Z",
    "2100-06-15T12:00:00Z",
});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, centuries.is_leap_year());

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[false, true, false]

Example 3: Scalar Rank Is Preserved¶

const auto leap_day =
    pluss::timeline::make("2024-02-29T23:59:59.999999999Z");
pluss::series::print(std::cout, leap_day.is_leap_year());

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=true

Use leap_scalar() when the receiver is rank zero and a native bool, rather than a rank-zero Series, is the desired result.

Example 4: Timezone Can Change The Year¶

const auto utc = pluss::timeline::make("2021-01-01T00:30:00Z");
const auto local = utc.tz_convert("America/New_York");
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "UTC=" << utc.is_leap_year().item<bool>() << '\n'
          << "New York=" << local.is_leap_year().item<bool>() << '\n';

UTC=false
New York=true

Both values represent one instant. It lies in 2021 in UTC and in 2020 in New York.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • false means either a common local year or NaT.

  • Time-of-day and month do not affect membership once the local year is known.

  • The method accepts every supported Timeline rank; it is not a reduction.

  • To identify leap day itself, combine month() == 2 with day() == 29.
